# Quarto Presentation
This project explores how Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) can be used to represent and compress images. Although modern image compression such as jpeg rely on the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), as calculating SVD's becomes computationally expensive for large datastructures, SVD's remains as a good foundational concept for understanding image processing. Therefore, this presentation will give a introduction to the mathematics of image representation.

Below, you'll find two collapsed code blocks containing the pre-loaded packages and the raw data. Feel free to expand them if you want to inspect what is loaded. The raw data consists of pixel values ranging from $[0-15]$, representing a grayscale image.

## How an SVD works
Below is a simple example of how an SVD of the matrix $A$ would look like 
$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 2 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}
$$

The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of $A$ is given by

$$
A = U \Sigma V^T
$$

where

$$
U\Sigma V^T =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 0 \\
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-svd-matrix}

The dimensions of the matrices are therefore

$$
\underbrace{(3 \times 3)}_{U}
\underbrace{(3 \times 2)}_{\Sigma}
\underbrace{(2 \times 2)}_{V^T}
=
(3 \times 2).
$$

Thus, the SVD decomposes the original $3 \times 2$ matrix into three
matrices whose dimensions allow them to be multiplied back together to
reconstruct $A$. 

## The Low-Rank Approximation Problem
Now that we have seen the full SVD, we can explore what happens when we truncate it. This leads to a fundamental question known as the low-rank approximation problem: for a given rank $k$, how do we find a simpler matrix $A_k$ that is as close as possible to our original matrix $A$?  

The Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem provides the mathematical answer, the optimal rank-$k$ approximation is obtained simply by keeping the $k$ largest singular values and their corresponding singular vectors, while discarding the rest.

### Rank 1 example
Continuing from the SVD in @eq-svd-matrix, if we set the rank to $k = 1$, we keep only the first column of $U$, the first singular value of $\Sigma$, and the first row of $V^T$ giving us
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}= 2*
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}=
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$
This rank-1 matrix retains the same $3 \times 2$ dimensions, but it only captures the most dominant feature (the largest value, $2$) while omitting the rest.

### Rank 2 example
If we set $k = 2$, we include the second singular component giving us 
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
 \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
   = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$
Notice that the result is the exact original matrix $A$. Because $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and as the maximum possible rank is $2$. The $k = 2$ represents a full-rank reconstruction, meaning 100% of the original information is recovered.

Below is a larger version of this exact example, where you can play around with the rank.
```{pyodide-python}

(U, S, V) = linalg.svd(img)
# This runs an SVD on the img, splitting it into 3 parts:
# U: a unitary matrix (a complex square matrix whose inverse equals its conjugate transpose).
# S: a rectangular diagonal matrix with non-negative real numbers on the diagonal.
# V: also a unitary matrix.


ranks = [27, 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1] 
# These are the ranks chosen to recreate the image, going from 27 down to 1.
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
# Creates the canvas and plotting area.
im = ax.imshow(img)
# Draws the uncompressed image (img) and saves the plot object in im.
title = ax.set_title(f"Rank {ranks[0]}")
# Sets the starting title text using ranks[0], making the title "Rank 27".
def update(frame):
    # Function to update the plot for each animation frame.
    rank = ranks[frame]
    # Translates the frame number into the actual rank.
    imgCompressed = U[:, 0:rank] @ np.diag(S[0:rank]) @ V[0:rank, :]
    # The actual SVD reconstruction math explained above.
    im.set_data(imgCompressed)
    # Updates the displayed image with the newly compressed image data.
    title.set_text(f"Rank {rank}")
    # Updates the existing title object's text in place.
    return im, title
    # Hands back the two objects that changed in this frame.

ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ranks), interval=800, blit=False)
# Builds and starts the animation.
plt.show()
# Displays the figure.
```
For large images (which contain thousands of rows and columns), setting $k$ much smaller than the full rank allows us to recreate a recognizable image using only a fraction of the data. This idea is hopefully seen in these exampels.

```{pyodide-python}
(U, S, V) = linalg.svd(img2)


ranks = [27, 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im2 = ax.imshow(img2)
title = ax.set_title(f"Rank {ranks[0]}")

def update(frame):
    rank = ranks[frame]
    imgCompressed = U[:, 0:rank] @ np.diag(S[0:rank]) @ V[0:rank, :]
    im2.set_data(imgCompressed)
    title.set_text(f"Rank {rank}")
    return im2, title

ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ranks), interval=800, blit=False)
plt.show()
```
